utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Judge Morrison is indisposed today, so we will be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Good morning, Mr. Nicholls. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. Just preliminarily if I could correct an ambiguous line in the transcript from yesterday. At page 31354 when I was summarising the testimony of the witness in the Krajisnik trial, at lines 5 to 6 yesterday I said: "At the bottom of the page he talks about one of the detainees called Milorad Sehovac." I didn't say that very well. What it says in the transcript is that one of the detainees made a telephone call to military officer named Milorad Sehovac, that's what it says in the transcript, not that one of the detainees had that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good. Now, yesterday when we left off I was about to ask you a question and we ran out of time. But you said yesterday on page 31355 at line 5: "In paragraph 2 of my statement I stated exactly the period I was in Brcko, from mid-August 1991 to 15 August 1992." So could we please bring up your statement 1D06901. And I see you've got a hard copy in front of you, is that right, of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I would like to state the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Wait for the question -- wait for the question --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The question is: Where in your statement in paragraph -- where in paragraph 2 does it say you were in Brcko from -- at all, let alone in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I issued orders. I handed over five documents, some of which are originals. I handed them over to the Defence on the first day when I arrived and they were uploaded in the e-court of The Hague Tribunal. In addition to that, to tell the whole truth I can tell you that I have all the five copies of those orders. One of them is the certificate of the command of the East Bosnian Corps, which says expressly that from the 19th of May, 1991, until the 15th of August, 1992, I was a member of the East Bosnia Corps. Furthermore, I have the original of an order by the minister of defence of Republika Srpska, General Subotic, by which I was appointed the commander of the Sarajevo brigade. Furthermore, I enclosed the original discharge letter of the military academy from the 3rd to 9 July, 1995. And the fourth document that I submitted is an order pursuant to which I was transferred from the Main Staff of Republika Srpska to the Army of Yugoslavia. And the fifth document that I enclosed is an order by the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia dated 15 April 2002 by which I was pensioned off --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I handed all of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you understood the question. I'll ask Mr. Nicholls to repeat his question. Please concentrate on answering the question. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The question was: You said yesterday in this courtroom: "In paragraph 2 of your statement I stated exactly the period when I was in Brcko, from mid-August 1991 until 15 August 1992." Understand, I'm not disputing that you were in Brcko during that period. My question is: Where in paragraph 2 of your statement does it say that? Do you agree with me, there's no mention of Brcko whatsoever in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only reason for that is the fact that as I followed the situation, I saw that this was about Sarajevo, so I mentioned only those duties that I discharged in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So then you agree with me -- stop --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is the exclusive reason why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you agree that there's no mention about Brcko in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question -- Mr. Nicholls asked the question because you answered differently. You said yesterday it is included in your statement, which was not true now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I see you have your statement in front of you. I noticed yesterday when you were looking at it - and I didn't have time - that it appeared to have a lot of handwriting on the back pages, a lot of notes. Would you mind if I took a look at your statement, please, if I could have the assistance of the usher. Well, you showed me the last page is blank, but the back of page 1, for the record, has a lot of writing on it including something about Brcko. The back of page 2 has a whole bunch of stuff written about Brcko and I see Hrvati, Muslimani. The back of page 3 has a whole bunch of writing. The back of page 4 has about a third of the page writing. The back of page 5 is full of writing about Sarajevo. And there are other notes on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for a copy of this and I would have a colleague who can read Serbian read take a look at it while I continue my cross-examination. If I could make a photocopy with the usher's help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we need a break to copy it -- I don't mind if he needs the statement he feels for the rest of the questions, otherwise I can give him a clean copy of his statement in his language that has no writing on it, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.11 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, sir, just a couple more questions on this topic. Yesterday at page 31355 you said that from 9 until 20th of May you were in - and we have it written as Piparci - can you please spell that village where you say you were. Is it Piperci?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Piperci, P-i-p-e-r-c-i, east of Brcko in the direction of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 24347, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, I see you have your statement in front of you again. I have no problem with that, but if you need to refer to it let me know --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can return this statement. I have no need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me finish. You can keep it. Just if you want to refer to it, let me know so that we have a record of when you're testifying just from your memory and when you need it to check something. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand that, Your Honour, and I'll tell you why. I prepared myself for Sarajevo. After I had an interview with the Prosecutor's office two days ago, I wrote this down from memory about Brcko. In order to tell the truth here, I tried to remember some events and some dates. I prepared myself thoroughly for Sarajevo based on the materials that were available to me. For the Defence, I prepared myself exclusively for Sarajevo. That's the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Sehovac. When did you write down those handwritten notes on your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the interview with the Prosecutor. That conversation lasted for about 45 minutes. I thought that it would be necessary for me to try and remember as much as I could. At the end of the day I don't need this statement at all. You know, there were a lot of events 20 years ago and you have to remember everything. I changed two or three positions during the war and I was taken by surprise when I heard that Brcko would also be discussed as part of this Court's agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have any problem with you keeping the statement with you, but when you need to refer to your handwritten notes, please let us know. That's the only point Mr. Nicholls was making.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Now I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a map of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it wasn't on my list, Your Honours, but I didn't know this name would come up. I've provided it to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, could you take a look at the map here. You said Piperci was just east of Brcko. I think you'll be able to find it on this map. Could you just circle it with a pen and the usher will help you do that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's, what, about 30 kilometres from Brcko roughly or perhaps less?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you start measuring from the entrance into the city, it's about 20 kilometres. From the barracks, it's about 24 to 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You've answered the question. If you could just put your name on this map at the bottom and put the date, which is December 13th, 2012.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My full name or just my initials?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think your initials are fine.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't work. Today is the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6043, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm moving on to a different subject, sir, and that is about Sarajevo, which you prepared yourself for, and I'm going to ask you some questions beginning with paragraph 63 of your statement which you can look at if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it you gave your first statement to the Defence approximately a year ago, December 2011; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then when you came to The Hague you added to your statement and that was recently, this month, when you arrived here; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reason why I added things --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, please, please --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was that I had prepared myself in the meantime and I arrived with correct information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. When I ask you a question that can be answered with either yes or no like: Did you add material to your statement when you arrived? The answer to that is, if you did do it, yes. And you don't need to then explain more unless it's a -- unless it's a question that can't be answered with yes or no. So I'll give you a chance to explain your answers, but try to listen to the question and just answer the question I ask and not go further. Now, we were given a track changes version of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I could have the statement up, please, at paragraph 63, which is page 19 in English, page 12 in the Serbian original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the first -- I'll call it the first version of your statement, the 2011 version, only included the first three sentences. So it read only, and I'll read it: "I was shown document 1D8436 - the document that I compiled is about military targets in the centre of Hrasnica. In connection with this I was shown document 65 ter 10693 which relates to the military targets that I identified in document 1D8436. According to my information, a modified aerial bomb was fired on the Aleksa Santic school, where shells were produced for the use of the 1st K of the BH Army."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we bring that up, please. It's D02353.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So I believe the correct number for the document you referred to. That's the document that you were discussing, your document from August 1994, your analysis of defence line, correct, that's the document you were referring to in your statement as of 2011?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The order to launch the air bombs that you referred to was on 6 April 1995, eight months after your analysis. That's an eight-month gap between the time of your analysis and the time of the order to launch, but you still link those two documents. That's what your statement says; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the one who issued the order to launch the air bomb --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There may be --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There may be a translation error. I know you didn't issue the order to launch the air bomb. What I'm saying is according to your statement these documents related, even though there's an eight-month gap between your analysis and the order to launch the air bomb, which was not issued by you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now you arrive in The Hague one year later and we look at the rest of paragraph 63, the widely expanded story you have on the reasoning for the launching of the air bomb on Hrasnica. And you have now included additional documents P5981, document D782, which you say sheds light on the order from General Milosevic for the fire of the air bomb. And you've concluded that you have information that the fired air bomb landed near the Aleksa Santic school where ammunition was manufactured, tying it back to your statement a year earlier. Where did you get your information from that the air bomb landed near the Aleksa Santic school? That's not clear from your statement.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, from my observation post you can see all of Hrasnica almost. We heard that there was a launch and we saw it. Also we heard from the corps command that the bomb has -- had landed in the sector of the target. And thirdly, something that I would like to emphasize, nothing changed from the moment when I sent my analysis to the moment the bomb was launched. All that time ammunition was being manufactured there; in other words, by observation and through information from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. At the moment when the bomb was launched, my brigade had suffered very strong attacks from the Hrasnica sector that had lasted for the two or three previous days. I don't know whether you know that during combat activities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, could you concentrate on answering the question. The question was whether you -- where you got your information from that the air bomb landed near Aleksa Santic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you've answered that. Thank you, sir. So just so I understand, from line of sight from your position when the air bomb landed you could see Hrasnica and see where the bomb had landed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So then you would have been able to see immediately that it had not hit the school which was the supposed target; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from a distance of some 3 kilometres according to what I saw it was 20 to 30 metres away from it, but you really can't pin-point the distance to the last metre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So to answer my question, the answer is: Yes, you could see that it missed the target?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could see that it landed in the immediate vicinity of the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you couldn't see that the school was still standing? You just told me: "According to what I saw, it was 20 to 30 metres away from it." So -- and our position is that it was a lot farther away from it than that, it was 148 metres roughly. But answer the question: You could see that it had not hit the school; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but it landed in the vicinity of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have D00782.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this document you refer to in paragraph 63 saying: "This was shown to me," by the Defence, "sheds light on the order from General Milosevic for the fire of the air bomb as a response from enemy fire..." This order for artillery is for Lukavac 95; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you can read "Lukavac 95" on the right top part of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the year is 1995 and the combat was going on on the Igman-Trnovo axis. That's what the commander stated in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's dated 4 April 1995. You say it relates to the order to launch the air bomb on 6 April. I think we can agree this Lukavac 95 document says nothing whatsoever about the Aleksa Santic primary school. It talks only about neutralising the activity of the enemy artillery and mortars. Correct? This has nothing to do with your document from eight months earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like P01201, that's the 6th of April order. All right. This is the order we've been talking about. It's -- yes, thank you. It's an order, it's a pretty clear order, and it gives the reason for the order. In the first paragraph Muslim forces have been attacking from the positions of the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade ... et cetera, several of our soldiers and a number of our civilians have been wounded. "In order to thwart the enemy and give them a warning so they are forced to accept this truce, I hereby order: "The Ilidza Brigade will immediately prepare a launcher with an aerial bomb and transport the bomb for launching. "Select the highest-yielding target in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Kolonija, where there will be the greatest human and material losses." So first this order is not even limited to Hrasnica, is it, and where the air bomb should be launched? It also allows for Sokolovic Kolonija; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, therefore, having nothing to do with your order from eight months earlier. Now, we've already established that this air bomb missed the school. Do you know what damage it did as you sit here today? Do you know who it killed and what it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not issue any orders. I sent my proposal to the corps command for the use of an air bomb. Second of all, I don't know who it killed. I have some unofficial information that, inter alia, the soldiers who secured the command post and the factory that manufactured shells for the 1st Corps, that they were also killed. That among the casualties there were also soldiers, and I'm not contesting that there may have been collateral damage among civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. First of all, I apologise for calling your document an order. You're right, it was an analysis. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P01798, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a report of the forensic on-site investigation of that air bomb. It gives the location. And if you look at this, it lists Ziba Custovic, that's a woman, a Muslim woman, that was killed and the persons who were injured and shows that two homes were destroyed and 11 houses damaged. Now, our position is that this location is approximately 150 metres from the school. Do you accept that, that these were homes destroyed 150 metres from the target?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I answer? Well, you see, Fikret Prevljak was the commander of the 104th Brigade. His duty was to eliminate civilians from his deployment sector. Obviously he didn't do that. Second of all, at that time I was engaged with the 4th Motorised Brigade in infantry attacks. This was fought by the Ilidza Brigade, and I'm not contesting any of the things that I see written in this document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could I have P01201 back up, please. Try to follow me, sir. If you look at this order from General Milosevic, if we follow the plain meaning of it, it says launch a - an - aerial bomb, one. "Select the highest yielding target in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Kolonija where there will be the greatest human and material losses" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to intervene on the interpretation or translation. Esteemed Mr. Nicholls said "plain meaning" and in Serbian we did not get a proper interpretation. The word "plain" was omitted and only "meaning" was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. I'll ask the question again then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The plain - or clear and literal - meaning of this document is to launch one aerial bomb at a target in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Kolonija where there will be the greatest human and material losses. Now, if that was the meaning and the purpose of the order, the order was accomplished, the mission was accomplished; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. However, there were military targets in Hrasnica and in Sokolovic Kolonija. In Hrasnica those were in the school, training of the police and production of shells, the command post in the direct vicinity, and artillery weapons --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe these are legitimate military targets and that's what I wrote in my proposal to the corps commander and that was on the screen recently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sokolovic Kolonija is missing from the record, when he was enumerating what targets existed in Sokolovic Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Try to answer your questions a bit slower, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, do you confirm that you mentioned Sokolovic Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Chamber understanding your testimony more correctly, please slow down when answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Exactly in your last answer there were military targets in this area. And you're a career military man from 1974 through 2002. If the order was to destroy military targets, if the order was to stop the -- to hit military mortars of the ABiH, then normally what happens is you keep firing until that military target is destroyed. We've seen video here - if I can't read the P number - P930, which shows the destruction of the Marsal Tito barracks. And we can see a shell landing nearby, there's target acquisitions, the shells get closer, the target is found, the Marsal Tito barracks, a completely legitimate military target, is obliterated by precise firing. That didn't happen here. You could see that the target was missed. If the object was to hit the school where weapons were being made, why didn't you fire again and hit the school? Not you but the 1st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was not the one who launched that bomb. I did not determine the elements. I only made a proposal of legal military targets. I think this question is superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only observe where it landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll take that answer. Have you ever seen an order -- this is a hypothetical. There's a sniper on a roof firing at your troops. Have you ever seen an order that says: Go after that sniper, take one shot at him with one bullet, and then stop?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want the interpretation to be correct. Shoot him with only round and then stop. The question cannot be answered properly by the witness if the question is not interpreted properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you want me to imagine a sniper on a roof and myself giving an order to my sniper to hit him with one bullet? I can imagine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then if you miss the sniper, you just let him keep continuing firing at your troops and wouldn't take another shot at it; that's your answer? Let the military target that's threatening you continue to exist?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the sniper is destroying my personnel and inflicting losses, I would order continued action until the target is neutralised or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you. And just for the record, the exhibits yesterday which I showed, the excerpt from the Krajisnik judgement and the transcript of the testimony in that case, I do not propose to admit those. I think I read the relevant portions into the record and I think my summary of the transcript was fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel Sehovac.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The testimony of one fireman from Brcko was put to you yesterday. That fireman stated allegedly that you had ordered some murders. He testified on 20th April 2004. That's on page 93 of yesterday's LiveNote. Did you after that date have an interview with the OTP; and if you did, do you remember where?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any interviews with the Prosecution, so we cannot discuss any dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any encounters, talks, with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here in The Hague roughly in 1997. I was invited by I think he was called senior prosecutor, Mr. Barry Hogan. He invited me twice for talks at the offices of the Prosecution in Belgrade and he asked me to be a Prosecution witness in the trial of General Dragomir Milosevic; however, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In what year did you meet with the Prosecution in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was July 1997. Please do not hold it against me. I don't remember exactly, but they must have records with exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would now like to have played T000-5525-2-A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an audio recording. I'm not sure. We'll provide a number now. We expected that this would be a topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is it related to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is related to the first questions about Brcko and the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, we should look at the date and year of the interview. There is also an English translation in parallel. Could it be played from -- first of all, let's hear the date and then we'll move to the passage that is important to us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Okay. I'll just repeat the last question --" "The time is 9.27 a.m., still the 11th of August, 2006. The tape is being started again at..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that the date was 11 August 1996 -- 2006?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we play that part again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "The time is 9.27 a.m., still the 11th of August, 2006. The tape is being started again after the phone has been unplugged. "Okay. I'll just repeat" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree or rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is a noise from which we couldn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreter's couldn't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Somebody's headphones are too close to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear on the recording that the date was 11 August 2006?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now listen to starting from 5.20. to 7.56.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "... and recommendations. I have a request to you or demand, [indiscernible] as you wish. First I am a suspect. I would like to know what am I suspected for. I would like -- what events am I suspected? I would like to know what time-period am I suspected? Fifteen years have gone since the beginning of the war and twelve years since the abolition of the war. I would like to give complete and full answers respecting you and the Tribunal, and therefore I would like to ask you to give me -- allow me certain time for preparation so I could give true, adequate, and [indiscernible]. "Okay. I'll try to -- I'll try answer your three questions. As far as what you are suspected of, it's a complicated matter but as I tried to explain the first time that we met, we are not suspecting you of any crimes. The Tribunal has no intentions of indicting you. The Tribunal is not actively investigating you in particular."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic or somebody please remove their headphones. They're too close to the microphones. The interpreters cannot work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Somebody's headphone is close to the microphone so that it makes some noises. The interpreters couldn't hear you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I change the side. Anyway, I am changing it very often. Is that better?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope so. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Colonel Sehovac, two years after the testimony that was put to you yesterday you had an interview with the OTP in which you were told that you were not suspected of any crime and there was no investigation against you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During this interview in Belgrade in 2006, were you asked anything about Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not asked anything because I asked for time to prepare and that time was granted; however, that did not happen. Still, I was warned that everything I say to the Prosecutors of the Tribunal would be copied to Zagreb, to Sarajevo, and to Belgrade, to the competent judicial authorities that deal with this type of crime. That's all I have to say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After that, did you have any other interviews with the Prosecution or encounters or talks - call them whatever you like?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not until two days ago here with Mr. Nicholls I believe his name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this exhibit and we will provide a transcript? 1D6831. We'll include the audio and the transcript or just the audio, as you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether it's really necessary, given that it's already reflected in our transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is so, then we can proceed the way you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to call --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 1D6825 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's switch to e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Colonel, you said earlier today that a year ago you handed over to the Prosecution -- to the Defence documents relating to your appointment and service in Brcko; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I handed them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are waiting for the document and for the interpretation too. Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a certificate from the military post 7102, that's the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, and it states that I -- could we move the text to the left, please - that I spent in military post 7410, Brcko, the period from 19 May 1992 to 15 August 1992, as I said in my statement. It's signed by Major-General Novica Simic, who was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say to the Defence team that you had been in Brcko and what did the Defence team say to you on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told the Defence team that I expected to discuss only Sarajevo and we had no special preparation for Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6825 receives number D2636, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one clarification. Could the parties take a look at line 17 on page 2 of the -- of today's transcript. To the question of Mr. Nicholls: "Where in your statement in paragraph 2 does it say you were in Brcko?" And he answered with this: "I issued orders. I handed over five documents, some of which are originals." By saying "I issued orders," I meant -- I take it that he meant to say that he handed over the five appointment orders. Would you agree in so understanding, Mr. Nicholls? Or shall I clarify with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's probably right, but I would prefer to clarify it, Your Honour, of what he handed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you understand the question? The transcript says that you said: "I issued orders ..." What did you mean by saying "orders" or issuing orders? Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be an error in interpretation. I handed over orders on appointment, some of which are in the original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- orders from my superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's sufficient. Thank you. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency, for this clarification. It's really useful. Can we now see 65 ter 24260.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you experience problems in Brcko with the forces that were active there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, especially with the paramilitaries and especially in the early days of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see paragraph 3 a bit larger in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And could you please explain what was going on and why in the sector of Brcko --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't want to object now, but I assume that this is -- this does not arise from my cross unless he's going to bring it somehow back to the cross. I mean the question of paramilitaries in Brcko and the problems he had do not arise from my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I tend to agree with your observation. But can I hear from you, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The cross-examination directly dealt with people who accused this witness of crimes, and I think the witness is allowed -- should be allowed to explain exactly what the situation was in Brcko and how, in fact, he was not guilty of any of these crimes. And we think that this goes towards showing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the question to be put.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, Colonel, tell us, is it true that you had been arrested along with president of the municipality of Brcko, members of the Executive Council, and demands were made to free those people who had been arrested by our police forces?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, because we opposed paramilitary forces, especially myself and the authorities of Brcko municipality. They arrested me and the president of the municipality and they held us hostage. And they would have probably killed both of us if it had not been for the protest of Priest Slavko who interceded. I want to emphasize that this was in July, the month when you sent a special unit headed by Dragan Andan, who we met with the military police, and started cleansing paramilitaries in town. We disarmed them later and we drove them to the border with Serbia and expelled them from Brcko. Do I need to clarify more?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's enough for now. Just tell us one more thing. You heard what is included in the Krajisnik judgement. Who, to the best of your knowledge, was the armed force at the time able to commit the crimes discussed by that fireman?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paramilitaries. To be quite clear, at that point in time in Brcko, there was a group of 20 of Arkan's men, about 30 men who were Captain Dragan's unit, then there were the Red Berets, then there was a group of eight to nine people from Zbor [phoen], and finally the so-called milicija Krajina arrived in Brcko. We had to deal with all of them and we cleansed them. Enormous problems we had, both we and the government organs. It was only after a curfew was imposed, after check-points were placed at exit and entry points into important facilities. Also when we banned weapons in government buildings, no one was allowed to enter government buildings if armed, then paramilitary units - and I would particularly like to point that out - attacked the police station four times. Now, what was the objective? The sealing of documents, passports, traffic licences, driver's licences, and so on. In such a situation we received assistance from the Supreme Command, this special unit, and that is how we managed to cleanse Brcko with the assistance of our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, sir. Now we are going to leave the topic of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber who it was that signed this report, this regular combat report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see it very well, Dragutin Ilic, Commander Colonel Dragutin Ilic, he's the commander of the Eastern Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit as Exhibit D2637.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will now go back to the Sarajevo period. Today you were asked about the time when you found out that in Sokolovic Kolonija, Hrasnica there were military targets, weapons, artillery, and so on. When was it that you first found out that -- actually, when did you first find out about the strength, infrastructure, and weaponry of the 4th Brigade of the BH army under the command of Fikret Prevljak?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I arrived in Vojkovici on the 15th of August. From the 15th of August until the 18th of August, I got to know the command, the combat deployment of our forces, the support forces, then how the logistics functioned, then how the communications and command functioned, and the unit as a whole. In addition to that -- okay. In addition to that, to the extent to which this was accessible to them, especially in the front, I was made aware of the strength, disposition, and structure of the enemy in front of us. I was also made aware of the deployment of support resources. There were four firing groups, battalion firing groups, and the brigade artillery group. That is what I'd have to say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just to correct Mr. Karadzic, he says at line 27 [sic], line 3: "Today you were asked about the time when you found out that in Sokolac ... there were military targets ... and so on. When was it that you first found out ... about the infrastructure ... of the brigade ...?" I didn't ask about the time that he first found out about military targets. I just talked about -- asked him about his analysis from 1994. But I didn't ask him when did you first find out that there were military targets in Hrasnica, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's go on. But you pointed out the time when he wrote down that analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So on that basis it's fair enough to ask the timing. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, from 1992 onwards, if you knew what all the things that Prevljak had were, why did you not target them every day; or rather, when did you target them and for what reasons?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- we did not target them every day. We targeted them at the moments when they fired at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's another reason too. We were trying to save ammunition because our ammunition resources were insufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D6272, could we please have that in e-court. And I would like to ask the usher to help the Colonel with the use of an electronic pen. Page 3 now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be enlarged a bit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, could you first tell us what this map depicts according to what you can read from it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map shows the deployment of units on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it show anything else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows units that are involved in defence and those that are attacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Whose units are attacking and whose units are involved in defence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot say. Could it be zoomed in? I can barely see it, it's so illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't understand how this arises from my cross, which units were attacking where in the wider area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I'm just going to restrict myself to asking Colonel Sehovac to mark for us here the area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just tell us how this arises from the cross-examination of Nicholls. What are you addressing -- what part of cross are you addressing now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it has to do with the position of that brigade that was suffering attacks or that was inferior, rather, and that was in a position to defend itself, and that was challenged, or rather, it was brought into question whether that was necessity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I draw this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, I'm not sure whether it arises from the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, can you reply to Dr. Karadzic's submission, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. It does not arise from the cross. I think what Dr. Karadzic is probably referring to is the order which said that the 2nd Brigade was coming under fire, which is given in the 6th of April order to fire the air bomb. And I'm not contesting that the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade was coming under fire, if that's what he is alleging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Nicholls' observation. Please move on to your next topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My next topic is to thank Colonel Sehovac for everything, including this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Sehovac. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go, but we will rise all together. The Chamber will have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Katic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have a request for you and for myself, that we pause between my questions and your answers so that we would spare our interpreters. It is so important for us to have every word interpreted and we want them to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 169628, could we please have that -- 1D6908. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the statement, the one that you see before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read it and do you see that it correctly reflects everything you said?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions today, would your answers contained in this statement basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender the 92 ter package, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Actually, we're going to tender only three of these associated exhibits. First of all, 1D6905 and 6906, and we would like to have permission to add those to our 65 ter list as they weren't available to us at the time we filed that list. And then 1D08574 we'll also be tendering. The others we will not be tendering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards 1D8574, if you look at paragraph 14 of the witness's statement, he refers to item 9 and 13 of that document. How voluminous was -- is that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a nine-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are tendering in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, if the Prosecution wants it to be redacted, we'll do that, but it didn't seem necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First -- shall we give the number for the statement first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6908 receives number D2651, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. McKenna. Do you have any objection to admitting in its entirety 1D8574?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I have no objection to the admission of that document in its entirety. I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll give the number for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D8574 receives number D2652, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then we have two documents, 6905 and 6906. Do we have English translation for those documents? Ms. McKenna, were you able to see the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I wasn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So -- I couldn't see either, so in order for Mr. Karadzic to tender these two documents I would like him to lead live with the witness. Would you like to add anything, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may just add in paragraph 6 of Mr. Katic's statement, he refers to paragraph 39 of a previous statement. I think this is probably simply a typographical error. But I would request that Mr. Karadzic clarify this with the witness live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Fair enough. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if you could look at 6905, it's just a list so do you need a translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If I may add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see the document first. Oh. Can you read the document, Mr. Robinson? It's in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah, I realise that, but I -- in other words, you would like the names in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, if we are going to tender those, we have to read the names at least. I can read some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I know you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But not the all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Okay. We can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or -- but, yeah, he can put some foundation questions about the title and then we can mark them for identification. Where were we? I've forgotten. Yes, do you have any observation as to the observation by Ms. McKenna that Mr. Karadzic need to clarify live as to paragraph 39 referred to in para 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a good idea. He can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm advised that the Serbian version of paragraph 6 doesn't refer to paragraph 39 and apparently it's a mistake in the English translation. So it wouldn't be of much use to clarify it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to read out the summary of Mr. Milorad Katic's statement. I'll read it out in English. [In English] Milorad Katic was born on 26 of January 1954 in Sarajevo. In June 1979 he graduated from the mechanical engineering faculty at the University of Sarajevo and he started to work at the Put Sarajevo construction company. He was conscripted to military service in December 1979 and completed his service in November 1980. After the Put Sarajevo construction company, Mr. Katic worked for Famos factory, and later on for the similar factory Pretis, as a director of one production department. He was a member of the SDS board in Novo Sarajevo municipality in the period between 1990 and April 1992. From the outbreak of the war until 13th of March, 1993, he served as a soldier in the 3rd Battalion which became part of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. On 13th of March, 1993, Mr. Katic was appointed president of the Assembly in Srpsko Novo Sarajevo. In the summer of 1992, chaos reigned in the political system in BH and had been -- BH had been dissolved. When the Serbian organs came to power, crimes of all kinds were reduced to a minimum, an undertaking which was supported by Dr. Karadzic. When Milorad Katic became president of Serbian Novo Sarajevo municipality, he enforced guarantees of pension and humanitarian aid to both Serbs and Muslims alike. Citizens of both Muslim and Croatian ethnicities were elected as commissioners in their respective buildings and they distributed humanitarian aid. Grbavica was constantly under artillery and sniper fire from the Muslim forces of the city of Sarajevo and there were a large number of civilian victims of all ethnicities on Grbavica and other parts of Serb Novo Sarajevo. Milorad Katic's administration buried all victims, regardless of their ethnicity in the same graveyard and each grave was recorded. Milorad Katic states that there was no persecution of non-Serbian civilians, there was no, and that -- at the 1.500 people of non-Serb ethnicity who remained living in Grbavica until the end of war which testifies -- which confirms that there was no persecution. Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik held meetings with other leaders of municipalities throughout the Republika Srpska. Neither the leadership of Pale nor Mr. Karadzic ever ordered that water and electricity supply be cut off to the Muslim part of the city. There were two public kitchens in Grbavica in which two meals were distributed daily to everyone, regardless of their ethnicity. The Serb part of Novo Sarajevo and parts of Ilidza did not receive adequate about the electricity. The Muslim side, however, received far more extensive humanitarian aid from the international organisations and the UNHCR. By handing over the control of the airport to the UN in June 1992, the Serbs could no longer control the distribution of the humanitarian aid. Milorad Katic has never heard of a Variant A and B paper, nor was he aware of a meeting held in Holiday Inn hotel where the instructions were allegedly distributed. And that would be the summary. I would like to pose few confession to Mr. Katic, first concerning that document. [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D6905 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, could you please read the title and could you explain to the Trial Chamber what the document is about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that, Mr. President. "People buried in the Catholic plot between 1992 and 1996." This document refers to the individuals who were killed or either died of natural causes in the territory of the municipality of Serbian Sarajevo, predominantly in Kovacici and in Grbavica. Those individuals were either killed by shelling or by sniper fire or, as I said at the beginning, they died of natural causes. I received this information from the St. Mark's burial public company in Sarajevo, or rather, in Serbian Sarajevo. During the war, the name of that company was Sons [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we also take a look at the second and third pages to see if you have any remarks. While we're waiting for this to happen, Mr. Katic, who bore the cost of the burials of those who could not pay themselves? Maybe listen to the floor for that name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: The costs were bore by the local community. In this specific case it was the municipality of Serbian new Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was a distinction made between citizens of different religious and ethnicity affiliations? Or were costs born for everybody?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: The costs were born for everybody. There were Serbs who did not have enough means, so the costs were born for the burial of Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. I would like to add something about this document. All those people were buried in Lukavica cemetery. They all had their plots and everybody can tell exactly where the Orthodox plot is, where the Catholic plot is, and where the Muslim plot is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katic. You came into power -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, did you decide that this should be admitted or do I have to tender it for admission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification pending English translation as D -- Exhibit D2653. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, given that the next document is the same format, can it be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us -- let the witness read the title at least so that we can understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D6906.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the title of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: "Individuals Buried in the Muslim Plot Between 1992 and 1996."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the causes of death by and large when it comes to these people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Just like with the previous document, I would like to repeat with regard to this document. The causes of death were either natural or killing by shelling or sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again I would like to look at the following two pages, page 2 and 3, to see if the witness has anything to add. And while we are waiting, Mr. Katic, did the families of these people know exactly where they were buried? Did they have to look for them at all?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: This is correct. They knew exactly where these people were buried because there was quite a clear distinction between Orthodox Muslim and Catholic plots in that cemetery in Lukavica. After the Dayton Accords, families came and they could if they wanted to do so exhume the mortal remains of their family members who were buried there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm tendering this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be marked for identification as Exhibit D2654.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just one more question for Mr. Katic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, is it true that both in the party and in the municipality -- I apologise. Strike that. You said you came into power in the municipality in 1993. What was the reason for the change in the composition of authorities in Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the authorities always wanted to do what was the best for the municipality at that moment. However, my personal opinion is that what the previous authorities did was not enough to prevent all the irregularities that were rife in the municipality at that moment. Those included the distribution of humanitarian aid, the distribution of pension moneys, and as I heard many times, people of other ethnic groups were not treated like Serb -- Serbs were. They had to leave Grbavica. They were persecuted and things like that. And that's why I became president on the 13th of March, 1993, I became the president of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. New authorities, young officials, are probably more propulsive and we were able -- better suited to do what we had to do so that all the inhabitants of the municipality received humanitarian aid, pensions, and everything else that befits a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about those who were in power before you, did they participate in crimes or, as you put it yourself, did they -- could they not prevent those crimes? Were younger people sought to prevent that? Were some active mistakes committed by the previous government in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I may object to that question. It was phrased in a leading manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat and rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The authorities before you, were they involved in the commission of crimes themselves?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I would also object on the ground that it's beyond the scope of the witness's statement and 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the accused is going to lead live with the witness, can he not ask the question clarifying his statement which is contained in his statement, for example, the reason for his election at that time, et cetera, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding would be that the evidence should still fall within the remit of the 65 ter summary, that is, the topics that were notified to the Prosecution; but we'll defer to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He was introduced as partial Rule 92 ter witness and then he can cover any topics as far as is relevant and notified in general terms, so I don't see any problem. So I will allow Mr. Karadzic to continue. Yes. Probably you need to pose your question again, but please do so in a not-leading manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question, therefore, is this: What was the sin of the previous government? Was it crimes or their inability to contain the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: In my statement I stated that at that time I was a soldier in Zlatiste. More specifically, I never heard that the previous authorities had done something that would have lead to the change of authorities. The authorities before me in Novo Sarajevo never committed any crimes. I claim that. And I believe that as far as your question is concerned more specifically, that they were not removed and replaced because they had been involved in some unlawful dealings, but simply they did not pay sufficient attention to the things such as the distribution of humanitarian aid, the distribution of pension moneys, and providing for all the conditions necessary for a normal life in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was your predecessor and what was his profession?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: My predecessor was Mr. Milivoj Prijic. I believe that he was a physician, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at this moment I have no further questions for the witness, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime I was able to check the B/C/S version of para 6 of this witness's statement, and if we are to redact the first line and two words in the second line, that would be consistent with the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll have to ask Ms. McKenna whether she is happy with that solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Defence is to upload the redacted version. Very well. Then that concludes your in-chief examination. As you have noted, Mr. Katic, that your evidence in chief in Mr. Karadzic's defence case was admitted in most form -- in most part in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you will be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Katic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, as I have limited time, I'd ask you to listen carefully to my questions and to answer them as accurately and as concisely as possible. I'd like to start with a brief clarificatory point in respect of your statement. When we met on Monday you clarified that in September or October 1990 you were elected as an SDS deputy to the Assembly of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could you clarify the position to which you were elected?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: What year? I did not understand your question. What year did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: 1990? That's when the first multi-party election took place in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, and I was elected as an MP or an Assembly member on behalf of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katic. And you served in this capacity until the outbreak of the conflict in April 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd first like to focus on the period of the outbreak of the conflict. At paragraph 8 of your statement you say: "I was never involved in arms distribution. Shooting was everywhere and people were panicking and asking where there were weapons. Everything was disorganised and the situation was chaotic." This is a reference to the period at the very start of the conflict, at the beginning of April 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case you described in detail how the arming at the start of the conflict took place. On the 4th of April, 1992, you lived - as you still do - in Ohridska Street in Vrace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And on that date you heard shots from Vrace memorial park and you understood that there were clashes between the police forces at the police school in Vrace; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And that was when the panic - which you describe in your statement today - broke out, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: And that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So after an hour or two, vehicles started coming with weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Vehicles with weapons did not start arriving. One vehicle arrived with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If I may have 65 ter number 24328, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, I'd just like to remind you of the testimony that you gave in the Dragomir Milosevic case on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we could have page 9 of this exhibit, please, or this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And at lines 9 to 10 of this page you state -- well, actually at line 7 you state: " ... as I said, people started to gather spontaneously and started asking for weapons because they panicked." And then you say: "And I can say that after an hour or two, vehicles started coming with weapons." Now, having reviewed your testimony, is it your position that, in fact, it was only one vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I can say that when it comes to Miljevici village where I live above the memorial park, only one vehicle arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. So panic-stricken people, including yourself, stood in queues by the truck, the vehicle, asking for weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And those who were being armed were not JNA members, they were just local members of the Territorial Defence and other people from the surrounding area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And arms continued to be distributed over the next three or four days; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether that was over the next three or four days. I'm sure that it was for another day. Arms were distributed at least for another day in the area where I resided.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 10 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Katic, I'd like to remind you of your testimony -- your previous testimony on this. At line 3 of this document you state. "These weapons were being distributed over the next three or four days ..." Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: If I stated that it was over the next three or four days, I suppose that I was right five years ago. As I'm sitting today -- here today, I know that it was distributed over the next one or two days. I wouldn't be so sure that it was over the next three or four days, so I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. You received automatic and semi-automatics -- excuse me, you and your neighbours received automatic and semi-automatic weapons; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Correct. Semi-automatic and automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And the trucks -- or the vehicle or vehicles that came from the army barracks at Lukavica, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe that it arrived from the military barracks in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And weapons were also being supplied from Pale, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: From Pale to the lower part of the city as we used to call it, i.e., to the area where I resided. No weapons could arrive directly by trucks. It may have stopped somewhere in the region of Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So just to clarify that point, you're saying that weapons went from Pale to Trebevic but not from Pale to your part of Novo Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: During that period a vehicle from Pale or from further afield could not reach Lukavica or Vrace or Miljevici because the road between Pale and Lukavica via Vrace was not passable. In other words, one part of that road was under the control of the Muslim police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, just to clarify this point, in your OTP statement that you gave previously, you stated: "Weapons were also coming from Pale," and that's at paragraph 53 of your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. So I'm just -- I'd just like you to clarify what you meant when you said "weapons were also coming from Pale."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: All these things that I've just said I confirm again because I said back then that people who were not armed from our territory went on foot across slopes, the slopes of Mount Trebevic, to the sector that could be reached by truck, a truck that was sent somewhere from Pale or from behind the lines.
