utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.41 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragicevic. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dragicevic, before you start giving evidence, I'd like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Under Rule -- under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragicevic. Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, and good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The two of us speak the same language which is why I need to ask you to make a pause after my question to allow the interpreters to interpret every single word of yours because all your words are important. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D6903 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see a statement in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the first page of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read this statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this statement contain everything you said and does the statement reflect your words correctly?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers to the same questions be the same?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: They would be the same to the last detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I am tendering this 92 ter package into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would ask permission for adding the three associated exhibits to the 65 ter list. We were not aware of these documents at the time we submitted our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I give the floor to Mr. Nicholls, first with respect to 65 ter number 01369, I take it that you are tendering only page in English version that contains the relevant part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would object to that, Your Honour. I mean, I -- it's not a very long document. I think for completeness we should have the whole of that article in. The Prosecution has no objection to -- if I'm talking about the correct -- yes, 01369. I would move that the entire article come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Aha. You object to the partial admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, it's not a very long document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not an objection to the admission itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I would like the document to come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, this is a Prosecution 65 ter number, so if they can take care of that, this 01369, it's a 65 ter document from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you mean by taking care of it? You translated only page 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, if they could upload it -- if they have a full translation, if they can upload that, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to the previous one, i.e., 1D6902 , it's a bit difficult to follow how this is relevant or of any probative value or forms indispensable and inseparable part of witness's statement. So, if necessary, I would like the accused to lead live with the witness with respect to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't want to interrupt you. I object to this document even being considered for admission. One, it probably shouldn't have been disclosed in the first place because it's a work product. It's all the legal impressions of an attorney. Two, as you said, under no circumstances would this have any relevance for the reason I just stated. It's the opinion of somebody who was working on a file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But -- of course we'll decide whether to admit it after hearing the evidence, but would it not be relevant to the credibility issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because that was my third point, is the way it's being admitted and what is being admitted is in a very misleading way. First of all, in paragraph 49 it states that this document, 1D6902, is related to an investigation that the Prosecution conducted against me. That's not true. This is not relevant to an OTP investigation into a prosecution against Mr. Dragicevic. That's just not correct. What this document represents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a -- I'm sorry to interrupt you. But that -- so if I order the Defence to lead live with respect to that paragraph, your concerns will be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour. I would just make one other point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That what this document represents, 1D6902, is a review of a file that was sent to the OTP, and the Defence have attached only the first two pages of this voluminous untranslated file. So for this analysis to have any meaning, Your Honours, I think even if it were to be admitted - which I would object to - would need the complete file in order to see whether you agree with the analysis here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let's deal with it when it arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, so I can just give Dr. Karadzic some advice about when we would use this document. Is it the position -- does the Prosecution intend to ask any questions concerning Gorazde municipality of this witness during its cross-examination? If it doesn't, I don't think we would need to bother with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not prepared to disclose one sentence of my cross at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we give the number of -- for the 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6903 receives number D2658, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll admit the 1D6094 [sic] as an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number D2659, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll admit 1D6902 -- no, no, I'm sorry, 65 ter number 1369 in its entirety, as requested by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And receives number D2660, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it with the assistance of the Prosecution, the entire translation will be uploaded very soon in due course. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted to say that only these two pages were disclosed to me with regard to the last document from paragraph 49. And now I would like to read the summary of Colonel Dragicevic's statement in English. [In English] Colonel Luka Dragicevic joined the VRS in July 1992 and in October 1992 he was appointed the commander of the Visegrad Brigade. In August 1993 he was appointed Chief of Staff to the Tactical Group Visegrad and at the end of November 1994 he was appointed assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs in Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. In the second half of 1991, JNA members were ordered to attend work in their own civilian clothing due to the attacks that had occurred against the JNA personnel by paramilitaries like Juka Prazina and his men. He received information that a large number of Muslims had been sent to Croatia and to the MUP in Croatia for military training. He further found out that the Patriotic League training centre had been set up in Igman mount as a result of the JNA increased combat-readiness amongst its troops. A mass exodus of the Muslim officers from JNA occurred in March/April 1992, when all left at their own request and were not expelled from the service due to their ethnicities. At the end of 1991, JNA officers were attacked in Slovenia and Croatia, with barracks being under blockade and supplies, water and electricity were cut off, and large number of the JNA were -- members were injured or killed. During their withdrawal from Croatia, the JNA was attacked in the BH primarily by the Green Berets and the Patriotic League. The main goal of the VRS was to defend and protect the people who were on the territory under its control. The strategy was not to seize all of B&H but to defend those parts which ethnically belonged to the Serbian people and to people who were in favour of preserving Yugoslavia. However, the strategy of the opposition was to capture -- the opposite side was to capture the whole Bosnia -- of BH which was the core of their offensive operations. The ethnic make-up of the population in Sarajevo and surrounding areas was such that the predominantly Serbian settlements were concentrated around the city centre. This situation existed naturally, no one created it recently. At the same time -- at that time when Luka Dragicevic joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, sanctions issued by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were in force against the Republika Srpska and there was a shortage of food, fuel, ammunition, particularly large-calibre artillery ammunition. Rigorous steps were taken to conserve ammunition and fuel and measures were taken to fortify the defence positions. When Colonel Dragicevic joined the -- he became -- he became aware of intelligence that a large-scale spring offensive was planned by BH army. Any truce signed by Muslim military or political representatives would allow their forces to strengthen their own position. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at this point did not have any reserve forces or free units. Between December 1994 and April 1995, there were continuous attacks in Sarajevo from the Muslim-controlled area of Sarajevo. Often at the BH army forces would open fire from schools, kindergartens, hospitals, and apartment buildings in civilian zones. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, to avoid civilian casualties, was requested to only fire at the enemy's visible firing points which were inflicting losses to the army or civilians on the Serb side. Due to the enemy offensive, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps considered it necessary to obtain some of the heavy weapons placed under the control of UNPROFOR. As soon as this occurred, the Serbian side was bombed by NATO even though none of the weapons taken had been used. Following this, there was a powerful offensive from the BH against the Serb positions. Higher commands forbid the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps beginning any operation against the UNPROFOR locations, even when they were being fired at from because locations -- from these locations by Muslim forces. As far as Colonel Luka Dragicevic is aware, neither the corps commander nor any higher- or lower-ranking commander ever issued any orders for combat operations against UNPROFOR unless the UNPROFOR forces attacked their units first. He does not know of any cases of war crimes committed in the zone of responsibility of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps whilst he was in command. He is not aware of any facilities used to hold civilian prisoners. Imprisoned members of the BH army were under the authority of the security organs. He did not hear of or read about any cases of maltreatment. Colonel Luka Dragicevic has knowledge about UNPROFOR members being imprisoned in the military sense, which was done pursuant to an order from the superior commands. It was communicated to them why they were being imprisoned and there were no reasons for conflicts or combat; it was a protective and defensive measure. There was no opportunity for the Serbian investigative organs to investigate specific events to confirm the other side's claims about Serbian responsibility for the specific incident. Any requests made by investigate -- made to investigate incidents by the mixed military commissions were refused by the Muslim side. The offer from the Serbian side to have Sarajevo be an open city was categorically rejected by the Muslim side. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps never cut off electricity, water, and gas supplies to the part of Sarajevo under Muslim control and humanitarian aid was never obstructed and passed whenever it was possible. [Interpretation] This would be the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, Colonel, sir, about something that falls within your purview of moral guidance and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P02691.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While you worked within this administration of the army, did you organise some training courses and seminars?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We did that actually most commonly at those times when conditions for combat were not as good, i.e., when there was the least likelihood for an enemy offensive. And that was usually during winter-time. We mostly carried out training in the area of moral guidance, legal affairs, and Serbian traditions. And that happened usually in February and March. The training was carried out and involved the command cadre, including platoon commanders, company commanders, battalion commanders, and their assistants for moral guidance, as well as brigade commanders. I apologise. And the objective of the training was to inform the command cadre who would then pass the knowledge on to their troops. We could not involve all of the troops in the corps into such training. And it all had to do with the building of combat morale, the rights of soldiers, informing them about rules of war, certain traditions, and so on and so forth. After that, there would be a gathering involving the highest levels of command at the brigade level, who had attended the training. That would be a seminar as a result of which we drew conclusions on how successful was the training, whether the objectives were achieved, whether there could be some improvement made, and conclusions that the lower-level command cadre as to what needed to be done at our level or lower levels with regard to the problems that were encountered in the units, and that hampered our struggle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here you report, or rather, you convey a lot of criticism that may be heard in the trenches by the troops.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: However, the gist of that document is our request upon the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the higher levels of the state leadership, the Supreme Command and the government, and that for this to be presented in this form or a somewhat more stringent form; and the objective was to start to deal with the problems that kept on piling up for years into the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that something was not recorded. Is it correct that you have just said that you also covered topics of the Law of War?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything that fell within the purview of legal services, the administration for morale, and in my department in the corps command, because I was in charge of morale guidance, of law, and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I have no further questions for Colonel Dragicevic at this moment and the document that I have used has already been admitted as tendered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I take it para that 49 should be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, although we are reserving the right to use that document in re-direct examination but we can redact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we can redact the paragraph from the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Dragicevic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief was admitted in most part in writing and you'll be further cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've testified here in this Tribunal before; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On the 26th and the 27th of March, 2007?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In the Dragomir Milosevic case, for which you were subpoenaed or summoned to come and testify?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You began that testimony by taking a solemn declaration to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just like today?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were truthful in that prior testimony, were you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I was truthful. I related the information that I had at the time. I was truthful then and I will be truthful today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good. I want to touch on something that Mr. Karadzic referred to in his summary. In your prior testimony you testified that regarding the entire time you were assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs in the SRK, you could not recall a single instance of a commander within the SRK reporting a criminal violation of the international laws of war to the military prosecutor. Correct? Not a single report?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Those were reports that were sent to the military prosecutor. That was not within my purview. I knew nothing of reports that may have been sent to the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 24297, please, e-court page 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is your prior testimony, sir, I'm going to read it out to you. It's in English so I'll read it out to you verbatim this is from T3983 of the transcript, 26th of March, 2007, lines 8 to 20. You're being questioned by Mr. Whiting. And he says: "I want to move on to a new topic now. "Q. During the time -- during the time that you were assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs from the beginning of December 1994 until the end of the war, do you recall any instances where a commander from the SRK reported a criminal violation of the international laws of war to the military prosecutor?" Answer, your answer: "I never learned of heard something like that happening in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in the period that you referred to. As far as I can remember, if there had been any such thing in these reports from the Prosecutor's office, then certainly officers from the command would have received information about that and appropriate measures would have been taken." So you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once a month we received information from the Prosecutor's office on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm going to stop you. The question was whether you stand by that information and you answered that question. You can answer these types of questions more on re-direct --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Nicholls kindly speak into the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, why don't we hear him out. Yes, please continue, Mr. Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I swore that I would say the whole truth, not only part of the truth. Part of the truth is not the whole truth. It is correct that we received information every month, a regular report about the issues that were dealt with by the military prosecutor, and that's how we learned whether there were problems or not that were to be dealt by the prosecutor's office. We only knew that based on the prosecutor's reports. We could not influence those. But rather, based on such reports we ourselves decided what needed to be done, so as to prevent any such future incidents or to punish something that may have occurred in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dragicevic, the question was not about the report from the prosecutor, military prosecutor. Rather, the question was about commander's report to the military prosecutor, and your answer was you never learned of -- heard of anything like that. Do you stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I want to move to a different topic and just quickly go through a bit of your military background. If we could have e-court pages 3 to 4 of the same document, we're on 65 ter 24297. I'm just going to go through a bit of your background. This is from your testimony at 3969: "You became a member of the VRS in the Army of Republika Srpska on the 19th July, 1992, and on that day you were appointed Chief of Staff of an infantry brigade in Visegrad. That infantry brigade was first known as the Visegrad Brigade, later known as the 2nd Light Infantry Podrinjska Brigade. When the Drina Corps was formed in November of 1992, that brigade became part of the Drina Corps. You were appointed commander of that brigade on the 26th of October, 1992, and you remained commander until August of 1993. At that time you were appointed head of staff of the Visegrad Tactical Group to co-ordinate the work of various brigades. "Is that all correct up to now?" And your answer is: "Yes, it is." So that's all a summary of your early career in the VRS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: It is perhaps not true that I was appointed Chief of Staff of the brigade the same day. I'm sure that order must have arrived a bit later because it was not possible that I be appointed the same day as Chief of Staff of the brigade, but the gist is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's look at some of your early work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 24333.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the 2nd of April, 1994, document from the Visegrad Tactical Group --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Nicholls kindly speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- to the command of the Drina Corps, and it's an order to intensify combat operations. And we can see under the main heading "order to intensify combat operations," that this is pursuant to a warning issued by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2, please, of the English, staying on page 1 of the Serbian. Sorry, page 2 of the Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, we can see that part of this order is to co-ordinate the actions from Ustipraca and those of the unit infiltrated in the region of Gojcevici. And then it says in number 3. "All actions from the Lisac facility to the village of Djakovica will be linked up and directly co-ordinated by Chief of Staff of the Tactical Group Lieutenant-Colonel Luka Dragicevic ..." And that's you, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to show you another document and then I'll ask you a question about these. But this order came down as we can see based on the order from the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: No. This order came from the commander of the Tactical Group Visegrad, Colonel Dragisa Masal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct. Can we go back to page 1. If you can see here under the main heading "order to intensify combat operations," it says that this is pursuant to a warning from the Main Staff, that's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: The commander of Tactical Group Visegrad received a warning from the Main Staff of the VRS and is now acting upon that warning and the orders contained therein from the Main Staff of the VRS. He's implementing that order, issuing his own orders to lower-level units in the spirit of that warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 24323.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a report from you to the command of the Visegrad Tactical Group from two days later, 4th of April, combat report. "1. A group of 15 combatants crossed over the Praca river on 3 of April, 1994, at about 1900 hours and reconnoitred the village Gojcevici. Nothing special was noticed. "On 4th of April, 1994, at 4.30 the same group will cross the Praca river and set the village of Gojcevici on fire, in line with the conditions of the village of Surovi ..." Signed by you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a genuine document?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Really quite soldierly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And it is talking about going and setting a village on fire. Do you know the ethnicity of the village of Gojcevici, of all the people who lived there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: This was a hamlet of only three houses -- in fact, it had three houses on the forward front line and there were no inhabitants there. It was the forward defence line of the 1st Division of Gorazde, of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we look at the next document, 65 ter 08105.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the next day. This document is again from you, an interim combat report, stating that you have liberated the village of Gojcevici; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, but let me just explain. We, in fact, conquered the first defence line of the enemy side, the sector that was in the village -- I mean, it's a village on the map and we have to use that term, but it was not actually a village in the sense that there were no people living there. There were just soldiers from the 1st Gorazde Division, and there was their military equipment. Let me just explain this about setting things on fire. There were three houses in that hamlet in the sector of their forward defence line. Those houses had been devastated and they were converted into strongholds of resistance. There were strong infantry assets there and in the previous period they even fired a Maljutka for there. I barely escaped such an attack from a Maljutka in the vehicle in which I was. So that position in Gojcevici was close to Surovo, which was their reserve position. That had been going on for one year and the distance between our lines was no more than 300 metres. In some places it was 100 metres. And for a year we had been reconnoitring each other, occasionally firing at each other, we knew very well what was going on on their forward line and they knew what we were doing on our line because you could see with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You say there was only three houses there. Let's look at 00242I. This is the census for 1981 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not translated, Your Honour, although we have a translation of the headings because it doesn't really need to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But we can see there at Gorazde. And if we go to the next page in the B/C/S, page 2, and actually to page 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we collapse the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That would be good, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can see on line 13 on the right is where it's numbered as Gojcevici. And if we turn -- this is the 1981 census, if we turn to the next page, continuing on line 1 we can see that this was an entirely Muslim village of 48 households. And you did attack it and burn it; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it 48 households or 48 people, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you're right, Your Honour, people. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But that sounds like more than three houses, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this is about year 1992, whereas the document you are showing is about 1981. I don't know how many people there were at the time, but I know that since 1981 a dam and a hydropower-plant had been built flooding a lot of the land so that many people must have moved out. I don't know how many people there were at the time, as I say, but I know that for a year before we came to Ustipraca and the time we went there, there was not a civilian, not one civilian, to be observed there. We never saw anyone. And there were no animals, such as cows, that are indispensable to the life of that population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you just look up a bit, sir, you'll see that this is 1991 - look at the top of the page there - not 1981.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I heard in my headset that it was 1981 possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, that was a --

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going into numbers of population. I believe you that this figure is correct, but the moment when we launched that offensive and for a year before that, there was not a single civilian there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender these four documents we've just gone through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would appreciate it if we used documents of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the federal state. This is a document of the Croatian state, that is the source. They were making documents on the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I maintain that this figure would be different and it's simply not all right to use another country's data when we have genuine data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It all goes to the weight and then it does not matter at the time of admission. And then it's for you to use proper documents if you find it necessary. We'll admit all of those four documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document -- I assume that first document is 24333 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- and not 24297.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We start from 24297.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry that one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Then document 24333 receives number P6046; document 24323 receives number P6047; document 08105 receives number P6048; and document 242I receives number P6049, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I want to move on quickly and talk about Operation Zvijezda, or "Star."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P01645, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from the Visegrad Tactical Group command. It's dated 11 April 1994, in other words, about a week on from the documents we've been looking at. It's signed by commander Dragisa Masal. We can see - I won't spend the time reading out the distribution list - but it's orders for further action to be taken as part of Operation - I'm sorry I can't pronounce it correctly - Zvijezda 94, or Star 94. And I want you to look at the bottom paragraph number 7. "I am forwarding you a message from the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Mladic, who visited our zone of combat operations on 10 April 1994: 'Keep pushing energetically onwards, pay no attention to what is going on around us. The Turks must disappear from these areas.'" Now, as a corps-level morale officer, you know when that type of sentence from the commander of the Main Staff is included, that is in order to encourage morale and tell the troops what they're fighting for; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: In that situation I was not assistant for morale. I was Chief of Staff of the tactical group and also commander of a combat group. This document was written by Colonel Dragisa Masal, group commander. As a subordinated commanding officer, I received this document and implemented everything that related to me, that is, the tasks that I had as commander of a combat group. And this language, that we should not pay attention, that is a reference to NATO air-strikes and to keep dissimulating so that they would not destroy us. You are coming closer to the side that is supported by NATO so by doing that you force them to strike at both if they want to strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, and the message from General Mladic for this operation is that the Turks - meaning Muslims - must disappear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Hey, if it's a translation error, that's one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we should stick to the original text. The Turks, when we say "Turks" or "Ustashas," these words have their own meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's for you to take up the issue, but Mr. Nicholls was quoting directly from the statement -- the document, "the Turks must disappear from these areas." So what is your question, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That that is the message from General Mladic, that the Turks must disappear from these areas. And when we see "Turks" in this type of document, it means Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, most probably Muslims. That was the usual, or rather, frequent not usual name used for Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I want to look at another document, 24285 is the 65 ter number. That's part of your records. If we look at page 2, that's promotion proposal. And one of the reasons given in order to give you a promotion is that during Operation Star 94, as the Visegrad Tactical Group Chief of Staff, you performed the duty of commander of the combat group which liberated this area. So my only question is: You were promoted for your work or there was a proposal to promote you for your work in Operation Star 94; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Not only in that operation, but throughout my work from 1992 to this date in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I said one of the reasons, plural. So the answer is yes; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I gave you my answer thoroughly, and that's the truth. I can't answer this question with a yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I admit this document or may I tender this document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24285 receives number P6050, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to go back to your testimony in the prior case. This is a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 24297 back up on the screen. This would be e-court page 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to read out to you from page 4069, lines 13 to 25, where you were asked a question by the Honourable Judge Harhoff in that case. "Q. I realise that you have not seen it or expressed any opinion on it, but you -- I think you said that you had heard about such bombs," and we're talking about modified air bombs here, "being used in -- from the ground; that is to say, that they are being launched with rocket launchers in a modified way. That's why we call them modified air bombs. So you heard about them; is that correct?" Your answer: "This description that you gave just now as to what this looks like is something that I first heard during my interview with the investigator; that is to say, on the 3rd of August last year. They actually told me what this was like. That was the first time I learned about this, from them, how these bombs were modified and how they were launched. I personally had never seen this weapon being used in that way, as in land launched." You were then asked about when you first heard of air bombs being launched from the ground in very precise questioning by the Prosecutor Alex Whiting. Could we go to e-court page 108, which is T 4074, that's the transcript page, lines 3 to 14. "Q. I really want to be precise here. Did you ever hear about modified air bombs being used by the SRK. "A. I never heard this term 'modified.' What I heard was that air bombs were being used. That's what I heard. "Q. And when you heard about air bombs being used, how were they being used? Were they being launched from the ground, or were they being dropped by airplanes? "A. I already said that during the interviews with the investigators, I heard for the first time that they had been launched from the ground. I wasn't familiar with that kind of weapon or the mode of its use, and I still don't know anything about it. That's when I heard for the first time that this bomb was being launched from the ground." That's your earlier testimony under oath. I want to now show you some documents that relate to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P01782, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the SRK command 7 April 1995 regular combat report --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry -- sorry. That's not the document I want P01309, please. P01309. That's correct coming up. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an SRK command preparation for action order Talas 1. All right. It's a preparatory order. Let's look at page 2 of the English, we can -- page 2 of the Serbian as well. The date of this document again is 21st April, 1995. Could you look at paragraph 2. "Proceed forthwith to prepare launchers and make sure that four to six aerial bombs can be launched simultaneously against a designated target, the condition being that they must hit the target, which means that provisions have to be made for more bombs so that in the event of a miss the next projectile lands on the target." This document refers to aerial bombs being launched from the ground - correct - the section I just read out?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't understand this. It's probably from the ground. It doesn't say so. I personally never saw this kind of asset. This document was drafted by the operations order in co-operation with the chief of artillery and so on and so forth. I never saw this type of asset, but I must say that an aerial bomb is a permissible asset and it was used by the JNA. And it was taken from their depot. The way it is launched, how it is launched, I don't know that, that's what I stated because I had never seen it, but I understand the principle because I am an officer whose specialty is to be an air officer. But whether the launcher's on the ground or on a vehicle, I don't know that because I never observed it being mounted --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: -- this was not my narrow specialty. I would have wished to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Did the RSK have the ability to drop aerial bombs from airplanes while you were there? Was there an operating air force, your specialty? The answer is no. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: There was a no-fly zone there. The corps opposite did not have any conditions put in place to use air force --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: -- i.e., it did not have military aircraft, military helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to the next page in each language, please. All right. Now, you're named in paragraph 6 as part of this order, correct, so you should have received this order?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now go to 24322. This is an SRK command highly confidential order firing at rapid intervention forces dated 2nd of September, 1995, it's type-signed by you, Luka Dragicevic. It states: "I hereby order: "1. Prepare artillery fire for support of the units according to the plan 'Talas 1,'" which we just looked at, "which was handed to you in July of this year." Paragraph 3 : "Igman and Ilidza infantry brigades will prepare A/B launchers which will be ready for taking over of military posts according to the plan Talas 1. Military post 1...," I'll skip a bit, "activities on targets 1 to 15." Further down a little bit you'll see: "Igman and Ilidza infantry brigades will prepare 2 FABs each of 250 and 105 kilogramme and load them onto the vehicles of the Igman Infantry Brigade and 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade which will also load from their own reserves four FABs of 250 and 105 ..." Below: "We suggest that the SRK command should deploy the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade A/B launcher, which is currently positioned in Trnovo for the activities from the direction of Lukavica." All right, this is your document, it's an order to prepare air bombs to be launched from the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I have already told you once that I personally never saw that asset, so I don't know whether it was to be launched from the ground or from elsewhere. Second of all, I did sign this document in the role -- I suppose that that was in the role of a duty operations officer. At the moment when the commander was not there, when he was not at the command so he couldn't sign himself, that duty operations officer has the right to sign a document of that kind. The document was compiled by the organs of the command, the operative organ, the chief of artillery of the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. In other words, they were all professionals. It was my task to sign such a document. They were not able to do it. It was only the person who at that moment stood in for the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. At that time, it was me acting as the duty operations officer in the centre. I apologise. The commander of the IKM. I was the commander of the forward command post 2, correct. Now it is correct. And I had my inner circle of command which also consisted of some people. There was no difference between us and the SRK. I was in charge of a smaller part of the corps. It was 51st [indiscernible] smaller in territorial terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: At my forward command post I also had the chief of artillery, and I also had the operative officer, the chief of communications, and so on and so forth who were all members of the forward command post and they compiled this document in professional terms and I had the right to sign it. I am not -- I was not a professional body. I was not a specialist either for the -- for artillery or communications. However, I played the role of the commander of the forward command post 2. That would be my integral answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We just agreed that the SRK could not shoot, launch, whatever you want to call it, air bombs from the air because you had no aircraft. Where else can they be launched from if not the ground, if it's not from the air? You didn't have submarines either. Where else could you launch them from if not the ground, if you don't have an air force?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: It's not either/or. I said what I know. I did not see how the launching of an aerial bomb was carried out, how that launcher was prepared. I did not see it personally, so I don't know the details, whether it was from the ground, from a lorry. I didn't see that and most probably it was not launched from an aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It wasn't launched from an aircraft. If it's launched from the back of a truck, isn't that still launching from the ground as opposed to from a plane?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: It's not from the air. I suppose that it was from the ground, but it could have been from a platform on the sea or on the river surface, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24322 receives number P6051, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I go to P01202, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This document is also about Talas 1. It's from the next day, 3rd of September, 1995, and it's also from you. It's urgent. It's a report from the brigade command, decision on conclusions and requests. On page 1 we can say it's good -- you say it's good that these attacks were not carried out. But I want to go to page 2 of both and look at part (C). Again, this is from you. "Aerial bombs --" (C)(2). "Aerial bombs and other ammunition kept in the 'Pretis' are to be urgently distributed to brigades for security reasons and possibility of prompt use. Probably it would not be possible to deliver these items when required." So you here are ordering air bombs being delivered to brigades for use when you have no aircraft. That means you're delivering -- you're ordering that they be delivered for use from being launched from the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: May I see the first page? I failed to notice the date when --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Certainly --

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: -- this decision, i.e., that report was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Certainly, it's 3rd September 1995, but you can look at the front page if you want to.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I believe you. The 3rd. Very well. Just a moment, please. So I was still acting as a commander of the IKM 2 of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember my question?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: This is not the way it was -- yes, I remember. I remember it very well. Your statement and your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: -- was not good for the following reason. This supply was not for a future use. It could have been if needed; however, at that moment for three or four days we had been bombarded by NATO. Pretis had been completely destroyed, and aerial bombs remained intact by accident. And since this was all in one place, this was distributed to brigades because they could stock them, they could stock them in depots so as to save them and so as to be distributed evenly. And that was the purpose of this order, i.e., of this document that you asked me about. It doesn't say anywhere here that they should be used. It says that if need be they could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Promptly, prompt use?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just tell me where -- a possibility of rapid use, not prompt use. It doesn't say "prompt use," it says "rapid."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I'm putting it to you, sir, you were not truthful when you testified here last time this -- for that Honourable Trial Chamber. I'll remind you what you said: "I already said during the interview with the investigators I heard for the first time -- during the interview with the investigators I heard for the first time they had been launched from the ground. I wasn't familiar with that kind of weapons or the mode of its use and I still don't know anything about it. That's when I heard for the first time that this bomb was being launched from the ground." We've looked at documents signed by you that describe what these bombs are and how they are to be launched. I suggest to you you tried to hide even your knowledge of air bombs, you tried to hide your knowledge of how they were used from the Trial Chamber last time you testified here. Let me read you one --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we make a decision in the interpretation. Is it "ground" or is it "soil" or "land"? So can the interpreters finally make a decision what term they're going to use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You may answer. This may help you. Let me show you one more thing you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 2427 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to answer the question that you put to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to focus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the time. Yes, proceed, Mr. Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I was telling the truth then and I'm telling the truth now. I'm still telling you that I never saw that asset in operation. I never saw any launchers, and I know so much about bombs that I can talk about them until cows come home, but the point of questioning so far was that that was an aerial bomb that was modified. I claim that it cannot be modified as a bomb; it can only be modified in terms of its use, whether it's launched, whether it's throwing, whether it's -- you cannot modify a bomb which has a 105 kilos of Trotol, any kind of modification or work on a bomb containing so much explosive is banned, and I'm repeating, I never saw it being launched so I can't lie. It's impossible for me to lie when I say that I did not see that. I apologise to you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have one last question for you today. You are trying to avoid answering the question and you're talking about seeing air bombs. What you testified to under oath last time you were here was that 2006 in your interview with the OTP was the first time that you heard that this type of bomb could be launched -- was launched from the ground, and that wasn't true; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Everything that I ever said has been the truth. What I'm saying here today is the truth, but whether you understand me or whether you want to understand me is an entirely different matter. I said then that I never saw an aerial bomb weighing 250 kilos. I personally was involved in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dragicevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- working with 50 to 100 kilos bombs, and as far as the principle is concerned -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn here for today. But the question was not whether you ever saw the aerial bomb yourself. We'll continue tomorrow. And, Mr. Dragicevic, I would like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony during the [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00. Yes.
